en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Robes 3.
The Third Training Rule on the Kathina.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain monk received an out-of-season robe-cloth.
While that robe was being made, it did not suffice.
Then that monk, having spread out the robe-cloth, smoothed it over and over again.
While wandering about inspecting the lodgings, the Blessed One saw that bhikkhu repeatedly stretching out and smoothing that robe.
Having seen him, he approached that bhikkhu and said to him:
“Bhikkhu, why are you stretching out this robe and smoothing it again and again?”
“Venerable sir, this non-season robe-cloth has come to me.
It is not enough when being made up.
Therefore, having spread out this robe-cloth, I am repeatedly smoothing it.”
“But do you have an expectation for a robe, monk?
“I do, Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, having accepted out-of-season robe-cloth, to set it aside while awaiting further robe-material.

At that time, the monks—thinking, “It has been permitted by the Blessed One to accept out-of-season robe-cloth and set it aside while awaiting further robe-material”—accepted out-of-season robe-cloths and set them aside for more than a month.
Those robes remained tied up as bundles on the robe-racks.
While wandering about the dwellings, the Venerable Ānanda saw those robes hanging on the robe-rack, tied up in bundles.
Having seen them, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, whose robes are these, hanging on the robe-rack, tied up in bundles?”
“Friends, our expectation for robe-cloth has been set aside because we have no robes for the [wrong] season.
“But friends, how long has it been since these robes were set aside?
“More than a month, friends.”
The Venerable Ānanda expressed his disapproval, grumbled, and complained, saying:
“How can these monks, having accepted out-of-season robe-cloth, store it for more than a month?
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having rebuked those monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. …pe…
“Is it true, monks, that the monks, having received out-of-season robe-cloth, store it for more than a month?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
“How, monks, can those foolish men, having accepted an out-of-season robe, store it for more than a month?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...

And so, monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘If a monk accepts an out-of-season robe, he may keep it for at most one month. Should he keep it longer than that, there is an offense of wrong-doing.’”
“When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if an out-of-season robe should accrue to a monk, that monk may accept it if he so desires.
Having accepted it, he must have it made up quickly.
If it is not sufficient, that monk may keep that robe for at most one month, provided there is hope for its completion.
If he should keep it longer than that, even with the expectation of [obtaining] a robe, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*nissaggiya pācittiya*).
"When the robe is finished" means:
for a monk, the robe has been made, or it has been lost, or ruined, or burnt, or the expectation of obtaining a robe has ceased.
"Regarding 'when the kaṭhina has been removed':
it has been removed according to one of the eight headings, or it has been removed prematurely by the Saṅgha.
What is called 'out-of-season robe-cloth'?"
That which arises in the eleventh month when the kaṭhina has not been spread;
that which arises in the seventh month when the kaṭhina has been spread;
and that which is given specifically for a particular purpose even during the proper season—this is called "out-of-season robe-cloth" (akālacīvara).
"Would arise" means:
it would arise from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from relatives, or from friends, or from rag-robes, or from one's own wealth. "By one who desires" means:
[by one who wishes for it].
If one so desires, it may be accepted.
Having accepted it, it must be made up quickly;
that is, it must be made up within ten days.
"In the case of 'no completion,' that which is being made does not suffice.
That robe must be kept by the monk for at most one month."
It may be set aside for a maximum of one month.
"For the fulfillment of what is deficient" means for the purpose of completing what is deficient.
"With the expectation of a replacement" means there is an expectation from the Saṅgha, or from a group, or from relatives, or from friends, or of a rag-robe, or by means of one's own wealth.
If one should set aside more than that, even with the expectation of a replacement...
If, when the original robe has arisen on the tenth day, a robe expected as a replacement arises, it must be made up within ten days.
If, when the original robe has arisen on the eleventh day, a robe expected as a replacement arises, it must be made up within ten days.
If, when the original robe has arisen on the twelfth day... [and so forth].
...four days having passed...
five days having passed...
six days having passed...
...arisen seven days ago...
arisen eight days ago...
arisen nine days ago...
If, within ten days of the basic robe having arisen, an expected robe arises, it must be made up within ten days.
If it arises on the eleventh day... [and so on] ...if it arises on the twelfth day...
... on the thirteenth day after arising ...
on the fourteenth day after arising ...
on the fifteenth day after arising ...
When sixteen had arisen...
when seventeen had arisen...
when eighteen had arisen...

If an expected robe arises when the original robe has been obtained on the nineteenth day, it must be made up within ten days. If an expected robe arises when the original robe has been obtained on the twentieth day, it must be made up within nine days.
If an expected robe arises when the original robe has been obtained on the twenty-first day, it must be made up within eight days.
When twenty-two [kinds of knowledge] had arisen …pe… when twenty-three had arisen … when twenty-four had arisen …
When twenty-five had arisen...
when twenty-six had arisen...
when twenty-seven had arisen...
When the twenty-eighth [day] has passed...
when the twenty-ninth [day] has passed and the original robe has arisen, if a robe expected as a replacement arises, it may be used for one day...
when the thirtieth [day] has passed and the original robe has arisen, if a robe expected as a replacement arises, it must be determined on that very day, or assigned, or relinquished.
If he should resolve upon it, or designate it, or relinquish it, then at the rising of the sun on the thirty-first day, it becomes an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
It must be forfeited to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to an individual.
And thus, monks, should it be forfeited:
… [as before] … “Venerable sir, this out-of-season robe-cloth of mine has exceeded one month and is thus subject to relinquishment;
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha. … [as before] …
"May he give," ... "may they give," ... "I give to the Venerable One."
When the original robe has arisen from an unrelated source and an expected robe arises, and the nights [of the month] still remain, one need not have it made against one's will.
If the month has passed and one perceives that it has passed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If the month has passed and one is in doubt, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If more than a month has passed and he perceives it as not having passed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is not formally resolved upon and he perceives it as resolved upon … [and so on] … if it is not assigned and he perceives it as assigned.
Perceiving that something has been relinquished when it has not been relinquished;
perceiving that something is lost when it is not lost;
perceiving that something is destroyed when it is not destroyed.
If it has not been burnt, but he perceives that it has been burnt...
or if it has not been stolen, but he perceives that it has been stolen, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he uses a robe that has been forfeited without having first forfeited it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If the month has not elapsed, but he perceives that it has elapsed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If the month has not elapsed, but he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If the month has not elapsed, and he perceives that it has not elapsed, there is no offense.

There is no offense if, within a month, he resolves [the robe], assigns it, gives it away, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is burned, they take it after having snatched it away, they take it on trust,
or in the case of one who is insane.
"Of the first offender":
thus ends the third training rule on the kaṭhina, the third.
